about: THE REALM OF THE FRANKS, 780-1070: the kingdom and empire of Charles and Louis, then the middle kingdom that held Frisia (843-869), West Francia, Flanders, Brittany and Normandy. Written 4 Oct 2026 for the dialogue and card writers. rulers: one row per ruler and per 'part' (see parts), so the game can say who is king and who is the lord on the spot in any year; from/to are years. ports: which king line and which local lord each Frankish port id of ports_793.json answers to, span by span. raids: 'where' is a port id from ports_793.json when the place is one, else a plain place name with 'near' (the nearest port id). Sources are the annals by year, as in chronicle_793.json; modern works by author and year. (?) marks what could not be checked against the text itself, or where the sources disagree. All dates Julian. Northmen and Danes are the sources' words; the word viking is not used.

parts.franks: the whole kingdom and empire, to 840
parts.middle: Lothar's kingdom, 840/843-869: Frisia, the Rhine delta, the Meuse, Cologne, Aachen
parts.lotharingia: what had been Lothar's kingdom, 870 onward: the king who holds Frisia, Utrecht, Nijmegen, Cologne. From 925 these are the kings of the East Franks and Germans; they are listed here only so that the Frisian and Rhine ports always have a king. Their own story is in frisia_lotharingia.json in this folder.
parts.frisia: the lord on the spot in Frisia and the Rhine mouths: Danish benefice-holders, then the counts in West Frisia (the later Holland). Listed here so that this file stands alone; frisia_lotharingia.json in this folder is the fuller account of Frisia, its bishops and dukes, and wins where the two differ
parts.neustria: the great lord between Seine and Loire, who holds Paris for or against the king (the Robertians)
parts.normandy: the counts of Rouen and dukes of the Normans, 911 onward
parts.breton_march: the Frankish counts at Nantes, to 851
parts.aquitaine: the kings and dukes south of the Loire (Bordeaux)

rulers.name: Charles (Charlemagne)
rulers.title: king of the Franks from 768, of the Lombards from 774, emperor from 25 December 800
rulers.seat: none fixed; the court moves between palaces; winters at Aachen from 794
rulers.how_ended: died at Aachen, 28 January 814, of a fever and pleurisy

rulers.name: Louis (the Pious)
rulers.title: emperor
rulers.seat: Aachen; also Ingelheim, Nijmegen, Compiegne, Thionville
rulers.how_ended: put down by his sons on the Field of Lies (June 833), restored at Saint-Denis 1 March 834; died 20 June 840 on an island in the Rhine by Ingelheim

rulers.name: Lothar I
rulers.title: emperor (co-emperor from 817); king of the middle kingdom by the treaty of Verdun, August 843
rulers.how_ended: shared his lands among his sons at Pruem, became a monk there and died six days later, 29 September 855

rulers.name: Lothar II
rulers.title: king (his kingdom is 'Lothar's', Lotharingia)
rulers.how_ended: died of fever at Piacenza, 8 August 869, with no lawful son; his uncles divided the kingdom at Meerssen, 8 August 870

rulers.name: Louis the German
rulers.title: king of the East Franks; by Meerssen holds Utrecht, two thirds of Frisia, Cologne, Aachen
rulers.how_ended: died at Frankfurt, 28 August 876. (Charles the Bald held the western share, with a third of Frisia, 870-877: see part west.)

rulers.name: Louis the Younger
rulers.title: king of the East Franks (Franconia, Saxony); all Lotharingia from the treaty of Ribemont, February 880
rulers.how_ended: died at Frankfurt, 20 January 882, while his army lay against the Northmen at Elsloo; the army went home

rulers.name: Charles the Fat
rulers.title: emperor (881); king of all the east from 882
rulers.how_ended: deposed at Tribur, November 887; died 13 January 888

rulers.name: Arnulf of Carinthia
rulers.title: king of the East Franks, emperor from 896
rulers.how_ended: died at Regensburg, 8 December 899

rulers.name: Zwentibold
rulers.title: king in Lotharingia under his father Arnulf
rulers.seat: none fixed; often on the Meuse and at Nijmegen
rulers.how_ended: killed fighting his own counts on the Meuse, 13 August 900
rulers.source: Regino 895, 900; OSU 88 (his charter for Utrecht's men at Deventer and Tiel, 24 June 896)

rulers.name: Louis the Child
rulers.title: king of the East Franks
rulers.how_ended: died 24 September 911, aged about eighteen, the last Carolingian in the east; the Lotharingian lords then chose the western king

rulers.name: Charles the Simple
rulers.title: king of the West Franks; holds Lotharingia from November 911 and calls himself 'king of the Franks'
rulers.seat: Laon; in Lotharingia Herstal, Aachen, Nijmegen
rulers.how_ended: deposed in the west in 922, a prisoner from 923; Henry I took Lotharingia between 923 and 925
rulers.source: Flodoard 922, 923, 925; treaty of Bonn, 7 November 921 (MGH Const. I no. 1); his charter for Count Dirk at Egmond, 15 June 922 (Oorkondenboek van Holland en Zeeland I no. 28) (?)

rulers.name: Henry I
rulers.title: king of the East Franks
rulers.how_ended: died at Memleben, 2 July 936

rulers.name: Otto I
rulers.title: king of the East Franks, emperor from 962
rulers.how_ended: died at Memleben, 7 May 973

rulers.name: Otto II
rulers.title: emperor
rulers.how_ended: died at Rome, 7 December 983

rulers.name: Otto III
rulers.title: king, emperor from 996
rulers.how_ended: died at Paterno, 23 or 24 January 1002

rulers.name: Henry II
rulers.title: king, emperor from 1014
rulers.how_ended: died at Grone, 13 July 1024

rulers.name: Conrad II
rulers.title: king, emperor from 1027
rulers.how_ended: died at Utrecht, 4 June 1039; his heart and bowels were buried there

rulers.name: Henry III
rulers.title: king, emperor from 1046
rulers.how_ended: died at Bodfeld, 5 October 1056

rulers.name: Henry IV
rulers.title: king (a child of six in 1056; his mother Agnes regent to 1062)
rulers.how_ended: forced to give up the crown by his son, 31 December 1105; died at Liege, 7 August 1106

rulers.name: Harald (Klak)
rulers.title: exiled king of the Danes, the emperor's man; holds the county of Ruestringen on the Weser mouth
rulers.how_ended: not surely named after his expulsion from Denmark in 827; a Harald was killed by the wardens of the Danish march in 852 as a suspected traitor (?)

rulers.name: Harald the Younger
rulers.title: Danish lord holding Dorestad in benefice with his brother Rorik under Louis; Walcheren and the places round it from Lothar, 841
rulers.how_ended: dead by 850; the Annals of Fulda say Rorik was then accused of treason and fled to Louis the German

rulers.name: Rorik
rulers.title: Danish lord holding Dorestad 'and other counties' from Lothar I, then Lothar II, then both Charles the Bald and Louis the German
rulers.how_ended: driven out for a time by the Cokingi in 867; last seen swearing to Louis the German at Aachen in 873; dead by 882, when his lands went to Godfrid. Who held his counties from 874 to 881 is not recorded

rulers.name: Godfrid
rulers.title: Danish sea-king, baptised, 'duke' in Frisia with the lands Rorik had held; married Gisela, daughter of Lothar II
rulers.how_ended: cut down at a parley at Herispich (Spijk, where Rhine and Waal part) by Count Henry's men and the Frisian count Gerulf, May or June 885; his men were killed across the Betuwe. He had asked the emperor for Koblenz, Andernach and Sinzig because of their wine, which the land given him did not grow

rulers.name: Gerulf
rulers.title: count in Frisia between the Vlie and the Rhine mouths (?)
rulers.how_ended: not named after King Arnulf's grant of lands at Tiel, Aalburg and between the Rhine and Suithardeshaga, 4 August 889; year of death unknown (?)
rulers.source: Regino 885; Arnulf's charter of 4 August 889 (MGH DD Arnulf no. 57) (?)

rulers.name: Dirk I
rulers.title: count in West Frisia (Kennemerland); founder of Egmond
rulers.how_ended: died about 928-939 (?); received the church of Egmond and its lands from Charles the Simple at Bladel, 15 June 922
rulers.source: charter of 922 (Oorkondenboek van Holland en Zeeland I no. 28) (?); Annales Egmundani

rulers.name: Dirk II
rulers.title: count in West Frisia
rulers.how_ended: died 6 May 988
rulers.source: Annales Egmundani; Otto III's charter of 25 August 985 making his fiefs his own (?)

rulers.name: Arnulf
rulers.title: count in West Frisia
rulers.how_ended: killed fighting the West Frisians at Winkel, 18 September 993

rulers.name: Dirk III
rulers.title: count in West Frisia (a child in 993; his mother Liutgard rules for him to about 1005); builds the fort at Vlaardingen and takes toll on the Merwede
rulers.how_ended: died 27 May 1039

rulers.name: Dirk IV
rulers.title: count in West Frisia
rulers.how_ended: killed at Dordrecht, 13 January 1049, by men of the bishops of Utrecht, Liege and Metz

rulers.name: Floris I
rulers.title: count in West Frisia
rulers.how_ended: killed resting under a tree at Nederhemert after a won fight, 28 June 1061

rulers.name: Dirk V
rulers.title: count in West Frisia (a child; his stepfather Robert 'the Frisian' of Flanders rules for him from 1063)
rulers.how_ended: died 17 June 1091

rulers.name: Charles the Bald
rulers.title: king of the West Franks (by Verdun, 843); king in Lotharingia from 869; emperor from 25 December 875
rulers.seat: none fixed; Compiegne, Quierzy, Attigny, Servais, Saint-Denis
rulers.how_ended: died 6 October 877 in a hut in the Alps below the Mont Cenis, coming back from Italy; the Annals of Saint-Bertin say his doctor poisoned him

rulers.name: Louis II (the Stammerer)
rulers.title: king of the West Franks
rulers.how_ended: died at Compiegne, 10 April 879

rulers.name: Louis III
rulers.title: king of the West Franks with his brother Carloman; by the sharing at Amiens (March 880) Francia and Neustria
rulers.how_ended: died at Saint-Denis, 5 August 882: riding after a girl he struck the lintel of a doorway

rulers.name: Carloman II
rulers.title: king of the West Franks with Louis III (Burgundy and Aquitaine); alone from August 882
rulers.how_ended: died in December 884, wounded by one of his own men at a boar hunt

rulers.name: Charles the Fat
rulers.title: emperor; taken as king by the West Franks at Ponthion, June 885
rulers.how_ended: deposed November 887; died 13 January 888

rulers.name: Odo
rulers.title: king of the West Franks (count of Paris, not a Carolingian)
rulers.how_ended: died at La Fere on the Oise, 1 January 898, leaving the kingdom to Charles

rulers.name: Charles III (the Simple)
rulers.title: king of the West Franks (crowned against Odo at Reims, 28 January 893; sole king from 898)
rulers.how_ended: his lords made Robert king in June 922; beaten at Soissons 923, then seized by Count Herbert of Vermandois; died a prisoner at Peronne, 7 October 929

rulers.name: Robert I
rulers.title: king of the West Franks (Odo's brother)
rulers.how_ended: killed in the battle of Soissons, 15 June 923, which his side won

rulers.name: Raoul (Rudolf) of Burgundy
rulers.title: king of the West Franks
rulers.how_ended: died at Auxerre, 14 or 15 January 936

rulers.name: Louis IV ('from over the sea')
rulers.title: king of the West Franks; brought back from King Aethelstan's court
rulers.how_ended: died at Reims, 10 September 954, after a fall from his horse

rulers.name: Lothair
rulers.title: king of the West Franks
rulers.how_ended: died at Laon, 2 March 986

rulers.name: Louis V
rulers.title: king of the West Franks, the last Carolingian
rulers.how_ended: died 21 or 22 May 987 after a hunting fall near Senlis; no son

rulers.name: Hugh Capet
rulers.title: king of the Franks (chosen at Senlis, crowned at Noyon 3 July 987) (?)
rulers.how_ended: died 24 October 996
rulers.source: Richer IV.11-13; Bates 1982 for the day (?)

rulers.name: Robert II (the Pious)
rulers.title: king of the Franks (crowned with his father, December 987)
rulers.how_ended: died at Melun, 20 July 1031

rulers.name: Henry I
rulers.title: king of the Franks
rulers.how_ended: died at Vitry-aux-Loges, 4 August 1060

rulers.name: Philip I
rulers.title: king of the Franks (a child of eight in 1060; Count Baldwin V of Flanders his guardian to 1067)
rulers.how_ended: died at Melun, 29 July 1108
rulers.source: coronation record of 23 May 1059; Orderic Vitalis XI

rulers.name: Robert the Strong
rulers.title: the king's count and commander between Seine and Loire (Anjou, Tours, Blois)
rulers.how_ended: killed at Brissarthe in 866, without helmet or mail, attacking Northmen shut in a stone church
rulers.source: MGH Capit. II no. 260 (missus, 853); AB 861, 866; Regino 867

rulers.name: Hugh the Abbot
rulers.title: lay abbot of Saint-Martin of Tours, the king's commander on the Loire
rulers.how_ended: died at Orleans, 12 May 886, during the siege of Paris

rulers.name: Odo, count of Paris
rulers.title: count of Paris from about 882; holds Paris in the siege of 885-886
rulers.how_ended: made king, 29 February 888 (see part west)

rulers.name: Robert, marquis of Neustria
rulers.title: count of Paris, lay abbot of Saint-Martin and Saint-Denis; the king's first man in the west
rulers.how_ended: made king against Charles the Simple, June 922 (see part west)

rulers.name: Hugh the Great
rulers.title: duke of the Franks (the title from 936)
rulers.how_ended: died at Dourdan, 16 or 17 June 956

rulers.name: Hugh Capet
rulers.title: duke of the Franks (recognised by the king in 960)
rulers.how_ended: made king, 987 (see part west)

rulers.name: Baldwin I ('Iron Arm')
rulers.title: count of the pagus of Flanders round Bruges, by gift of Charles the Bald
rulers.how_ended: died 879. (He ran off with the king's daughter Judith in 862; the bishops cut them off, the pope spoke for them, and they were married at Auxerre in 863.)
rulers.source: AB 862, 863; letters of Pope Nicholas I; Nicholas 1992

rulers.name: Baldwin II
rulers.title: count of Flanders; builds the forts at Bruges, Ghent, Saint-Omer, Ypres (?) against the Northmen; marries Aelfthryth, King Alfred's daughter
rulers.how_ended: died 10 September 918; buried at Saint Peter's, Ghent
rulers.source: AV 879-900; Folcwin, Gesta abbatum S. Bertini; Aethelweard, prologue

rulers.name: Arnulf I ('the Great')
rulers.title: count ('marquis') of Flanders; takes Arras and Montreuil
rulers.how_ended: died 27 March 965 (some lists say 964); King Lothair then seized Arras, Douai and Saint-Amand. His son Baldwin III ruled with him 958-962 and died of smallpox, 1 January 962.

rulers.name: Arnulf II
rulers.title: count of Flanders (a child; Baldwin Baldzo guardian)
rulers.how_ended: died 30 March 988 (987 in some lists) (?)

rulers.name: Baldwin IV ('the Bearded')
rulers.title: count of Flanders; holds Valenciennes and the Zeeland islands from the emperor (imperial Flanders)
rulers.how_ended: died 30 May 1035
rulers.source: Thietmar VI.29; Gesta episcoporum Cameracensium I.114-115, III; Nicholas 1992

rulers.name: Baldwin V ('of Lille')
rulers.title: count of Flanders; guardian of King Philip I, 1060-1067
rulers.how_ended: died at Lille, 1 September 1067
rulers.source: ASC (C, D, E) 1037-1052; WJ VII; Nicholas 1992

rulers.name: Baldwin VI
rulers.title: count of Flanders and (by his wife Richilde) of Hainaut
rulers.how_ended: died 17 July 1070
rulers.source: Galbert and later Flemish annals; Nicholas 1992

rulers.name: Arnulf III
rulers.title: count of Flanders (a boy)
rulers.how_ended: killed at Cassel, 22 February 1071, by the men of his uncle Robert 'the Frisian', who took the county
rulers.source: Lampert of Hersfeld 1071; Orderic Vitalis IV

rulers.name: Rollo (baptised Robert)
rulers.title: leader of the Northmen of the Seine; count at Rouen by King Charles's gift
rulers.how_ended: gave over to his son William about 927; died between 928 and 933
rulers.source: charter of Charles the Simple, 14 March 918; Flodoard 923-928; Flodoard HRE IV.14; Dudo II

rulers.name: William Longsword
rulers.title: count of Rouen, leader of the Northmen
rulers.how_ended: cut down at a parley with Arnulf of Flanders on an island in the Somme at Picquigny, 17 December 942
rulers.source: Flodoard 927, 933, 943; Dudo III; the Lament for William Longsword

rulers.name: Richard I ('the Fearless')
rulers.title: count of Rouen, marquis; 'duke' in later usage
rulers.how_ended: died at Fecamp, 20 November 996

rulers.name: Richard II ('the Good')
rulers.title: duke of the Normans (the title is in use in his charters)
rulers.how_ended: died at Fecamp, 23 August 1026
rulers.source: WJ V; Fauroux, Recueil des actes des ducs de Normandie (1961)

rulers.name: Richard III
rulers.title: duke of the Normans
rulers.how_ended: died 6 August 1027, suddenly; poison was said

rulers.name: Robert I ('the Magnificent')
rulers.title: duke of the Normans
rulers.how_ended: died at Nicaea, early July 1035, coming home from Jerusalem

rulers.name: William II ('the Bastard')
rulers.title: duke of the Normans (a boy of seven or eight in 1035); king of the English from 25 December 1066
rulers.how_ended: died at Rouen, 9 September 1087

rulers.name: Wido (Guy)
rulers.title: count and prefect of the Breton march
rulers.how_ended: not named after about 818 (?)
rulers.source: ARF 799; Alcuin, De virtutibus et vitiis (written for him)

rulers.name: Lambert I
rulers.title: count of Nantes, prefect of the march
rulers.how_ended: took Lothar's side, lost the county in 834 and died in Italy, 836 or 837

rulers.name: Ricwin, then Renaud of Herbauges, then Lambert II
rulers.title: counts of Nantes
rulers.how_ended: Ricwin fell at Fontenoy (841); Renaud was killed by Lambert II and the Bretons near Messac or Blain (May 843); Lambert II held or raided Nantes on and off until the king gave it to the Bretons in 851; he was killed in 852

rulers.name: Morvan (Murman)
rulers.title: king of the Bretons, so called by the Franks
rulers.seat: a hall in the woods by the Elle (?)
rulers.how_ended: killed in Louis's campaign of 818 by a man of the king's stable

rulers.name: Wihomarc
rulers.title: leader of the Breton rising
rulers.how_ended: submitted at Aachen in 825, went home and was killed in his own house by Count Lambert's men

rulers.name: Nominoe
rulers.title: the emperor's missus in Brittany, count of Vannes; from 843 his own master
rulers.how_ended: died on campaign near Vendome, 7 March 851
rulers.source: AB 843-851; Regino 837 (his appointment, misdated); Cartulary of Redon

rulers.name: Erispoe
rulers.title: king of the Bretons, with royal dress by Charles the Bald's gift; holds Rennes, Nantes and Retz from 851
rulers.how_ended: killed at an altar by his cousin Salomon and Almar, November 857

rulers.name: Salomon
rulers.title: king of the Bretons (a crown and gold circlet from Charles in 868); gains the land between Mayenne and Sarthe (863) and the Cotentin (867)
rulers.how_ended: blinded and killed by Pascweten, Gurvand and others, 28 June 874

rulers.name: Pascweten of Vannes and Gurvand of Rennes
rulers.title: rival counts; they fought each other, Pascweten with hired Northmen
rulers.how_ended: both dead by 876-877

rulers.name: Judicael and Alan (I)
rulers.title: rival counts, in the west and at Vannes
rulers.how_ended: Judicael fell fighting the Northmen about 888-890; Alan then beat them at Questembert and ruled alone

rulers.name: Alan I ('the Great')
rulers.title: king of the Bretons (so in his charters)
rulers.how_ended: died 907; no agreed heir
rulers.source: Regino 890; Cartulary of Redon; Chron. Nantes 21-23

rulers.name: Gourmaelon, count of Cornouaille
rulers.title: 'prince' of the Bretons
rulers.how_ended: gone by about 913-914, perhaps killed by the Northmen (?)

rulers.name: The Northmen of the Loire (Ragenold, then Incon)
rulers.title: masters of Nantes and of Brittany; Nantes granted them by Robert of Neustria in 921 and again in 927
rulers.how_ended: Bretons rose in 931 and killed the leader Felecan; Alan Barbetorte came back from England in 936 and took Nantes in 937; the last fort fell at Trans, 1 August 939

rulers.name: Alan II ('Barbetorte', Twisted-beard)
rulers.title: duke of the Bretons, count of Nantes
rulers.how_ended: died at Nantes, 952

rulers.name: Drogo
rulers.title: duke (a small child, under Theobald of Blois and Fulk of Anjou)
rulers.how_ended: died a child; the Chronicle of Nantes says his nurse killed him in the bath at Fulk's bidding (?)

rulers.name: Hoel I, then Guerech, counts of Nantes
rulers.title: counts of Nantes, claiming the duchy against the counts of Rennes
rulers.how_ended: Hoel was murdered about 981, Guerech died about 988 (?)

rulers.name: Conan I ('the Crooked'), count of Rennes
rulers.title: duke of the Bretons from 990
rulers.how_ended: killed at Conquereuil by Fulk Nerra of Anjou, 27 June 992

rulers.name: Geoffrey I
rulers.title: duke of the Bretons; married Hawise, sister of Richard II of Normandy
rulers.how_ended: died 20 November 1008 on the road home from Rome

rulers.name: Alan III
rulers.title: duke of the Bretons (a child; Richard II his guardian)
rulers.how_ended: died at Vimoutiers in Normandy, 1 October 1040; poison was said

rulers.name: Conan II
rulers.title: duke of the Bretons (a child to about 1047)
rulers.how_ended: died 11 December 1066 besieging Chateau-Gontier; poison was said

rulers.name: Hoel II of Cornouaille
rulers.title: duke of the Bretons by his wife Hawise

wars.who: Charles against the Saxons; the Frisians east of the Lauwers rise with them in 784 and 793
wars.what: Thirty-two years of campaigns, forced baptism and, at the end, whole districts carried off and resettled.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The Weser and Elbe are army roads, not trade roads. From 805 a Frankish merchant may go no further east than the king's named posts. Captives come on to the market; the Frisian terps east of the Lauwers lose churches and priests in 793.
wars.source: ARF 772-804; Einhard VK 7; MGH Capit. I no. 44 c. 7

wars.who: Charles against Godfred, king of the Danes
wars.what: Godfred brings his fleet to Sliesthorp (804), wrecks Reric and moves its merchants (808), builds the wall across the neck of Jutland, and sends 200 ships against Frisia (810). He is murdered; his nephew Hemming swears peace on the Eider (811).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The Frisian islands pay 100 pounds of silver. The king orders ships built on every river that runs to the sea and has the coast watched. Sliesthorp gains what Reric lost: the road to the Baltic now runs through the Danish king's toll.

wars.who: the Frankish counts of the march against the Bretons
wars.what: Campaigns in 786, 799, 811, 818 (Louis himself; Morvan killed), 822 and 824; Wihomarc killed in 825.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Nantes is a garrison town at the edge of the realm. Salt and wine move under the count's eye; beyond the Vilaine a Frank trades at his own risk.

wars.who: Louis the Pious against his sons Lothar, Pippin and Louis
wars.what: Two risings. On the Field of Lies (June 833) the emperor's army walks over to his sons; he is put down, does penance at Soissons, and is restored on 1 March 834.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The coast watch falls apart. In the very year of the restoration the Danes come by Utrecht to Dorestad; they come again in 835, 836 and 837. Louis blames his counts and orders a fleet, too late.

wars.who: Lothar against his brothers Louis the German and Charles the Bald
wars.what: Fontenoy, 25 June 841, a slaughter of Franks by Franks. The oaths of Strasbourg, 14 February 842. The treaty of Verdun, August 843: three kingdoms.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Lothar buys help by giving Walcheren to the Dane Harald. Rouen (841), Quentovic (842) and Nantes (843) are sacked with no king near. After Verdun a ship from Dorestad to Paris crosses a border: Frisia and the Meuse are Lothar's, the Seine is Charles's, Mainz is Louis's.

wars.who: Nominoe and Erispoe of the Bretons against Charles the Bald
wars.what: Bretons and Count Lambert kill Count Renaud (843). Charles is beaten at Ballon (22 November 845) and at Jengland (22 August 851). At Angers that autumn Erispoe gives his hands to the king and gets royal dress, Rennes, Nantes and Retz.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Nantes and the salt of the bay pass to a Breton king. The Loire mouth has no Frankish guard at all; the Northmen sit on Noirmoutier from 843.

wars.who: Charles the Bald against Pippin II of Aquitaine
wars.what: Twenty-six years of war for the land south of the Loire. Pippin is taken, shorn, escapes, joins the Northmen and is condemned at Pitres in 864.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Nobody guards the Garonne or the Charente. The Northmen row to Toulouse (844), kill the count of Bordeaux (845), take Bordeaux (848) and burn Melle, the kingdom's silver mine and mint (848).

wars.who: Louis the German against Charles the Bald
wars.what: Called in by western lords, Louis marches to the Loire in August 858. Charles has to leave his siege of the Northmen on the island of Oissel. The bishops under Hincmar refuse Louis and he goes home in January 859.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The Seine stays in the Northmen's hands for three more years. Paris is burned again in January 861 and merchants fleeing upriver by ship are run down and taken.

wars.who: Salomon of the Bretons, the Northmen of the Loire and Robert the Strong, by turns allies and enemies
wars.what: Each side hires Northmen against the other (862). Peace at Entrammes (863) and Compiegne (867) gives Salomon the land between Mayenne and Sarthe and the Cotentin. Robert the Strong is killed at Brissarthe (866).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The whole coast from the Vilaine to the Cotentin is Breton. On the Loire the price of peace is paid in kind: in 869 Salomon gives the Northmen 500 cows so that his men may gather their wine in Anjou.

wars.who: Charles the Bald and Louis the German over the kingdom of Lothar II
wars.what: Lothar II dies without a lawful son. Charles is crowned at Metz (9 September 869). At Meerssen (8 August 870) the uncles divide the kingdom: Louis gets Utrecht, Cologne, Aachen and two thirds of Frisia, Charles a third of Frisia and the west bank of the Meuse.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Rorik at Dorestad has two kings to satisfy: he treats with Charles at Nijmegen (870) and swears to Louis (873). Tolls and lords change along the Meuse and the Rhine mouths.

wars.who: the western kings against the eastern for the Rhine
wars.what: Charles the Bald is beaten at Andernach by Louis the Younger (8 October 876). By the treaty of Ribemont (February 880) all of Lothar's old kingdom goes to the east.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: From 880 to 911 Frisia, Utrecht, Nijmegen and Cologne have the eastern king. While the kings watch each other, the great army lies at Ghent.

wars.who: the great army of the Northmen in Francia
wars.what: It crosses from England in July 879, winters at Ghent, Courtrai, Elsloo, Conde, Amiens, Leuven and before Paris. Beaten at Saucourt (3 August 881), bought off at Asselt (882) and with 12,000 pounds (884), held at Paris (885-886), beaten at Montfaucon (24 June 888) and on the Dyle (891). Famine drives it over to Kent from Boulogne in 892.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Thirteen years in which no town between the Seine and the Rhine is safe in winter. Abbeys and bishops wall themselves in. Flanders gets its forts (Bruges, Ghent, Saint-Omer), and round those forts its later markets.

wars.who: King Odo against Charles the Simple
wars.what: Archbishop Fulk crowns the Carolingian boy at Reims (28 January 893). Four years of marching; in 897 Odo gives Charles a share and the succession.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Northmen back on the Seine in 896 find both kings busy. Charles stands godfather to the leader Hundeus (897).

wars.who: Baldwin II of Flanders against the king and the archbishop of Reims
wars.what: Baldwin seizes Arras and the abbey of Saint-Vaast; King Odo fails before Bruges (892). When the king gives Saint-Vaast to Archbishop Fulk, Baldwin's man Winemar kills the archbishop on the road (17 June 900).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The count, not the king, is master from the Canche to the Scheldt. His forts and his peace are what a ship at Bruges or Ghent relies on.

wars.who: Rollo's Northmen against Robert of Neustria, Richard of Burgundy and Ebles of Poitou
wars.what: Rollo is beaten under the walls of Chartres (20 July 911). In the autumn King Charles grants him Rouen and the land to the sea; he is baptised.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The Seine mouth has a lord whose interest is that ships come. Rouen fills again; within a lifetime it is the port where wine goes out to England and where northern plunder is sold.
wars.source: Dudo II.22-30; Flodoard HRE IV.14; charter of 14 March 918

wars.who: Charles the Simple, the Robertians, and Henry I of the East Franks
wars.what: Charles and Henry swear friendship on a ship moored in the middle of the Rhine at Bonn (7 November 921). The western lords make Robert king (922); Robert is killed at Soissons (15 June 923) but Charles is taken prisoner. Henry takes Lotharingia, 923-925.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: From 925 Frisia, Utrecht, Tiel, Deventer and Cologne belong to the German kingdom for good. The western king has no port north of the Scheldt.

wars.who: King Raoul and the northern counts against the Northmen of Rouen and of the Loire
wars.what: The Rouen men raid over the Oise and the Epte; Amiens and Arras burn (925). The Franks storm the fort at Eu (925). Raoul is wounded at Fauquembergues in Artois (926). Peace is bought with a levy raised across Francia and Burgundy (924, 926), and Rollo gains the Bessin and Maine (924).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The last general tribute. Normandy's border reaches the Bresle; the Channel coast from Eu to the Cotentin is the count of Rouen's by 933.

wars.who: the Bretons against the Northmen of the Loire
wars.what: A rising on Michaelmas 931 kills the leader Felecan. Alan Barbetorte lands from England (936), takes Nantes (937), and with the counts of Rennes and Maine storms the last camp at Trans (1 August 939).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Nantes had lain empty: Alan cut his way to the cathedral through thorns. The Loire mouth is a Christian port again and the salt road reopens.

wars.who: Arnulf I of Flanders against Herluin of Montreuil and the Normans
wars.what: Arnulf takes Montreuil by treachery and ships Herluin's wife and sons to King Aethelstan (939); Herluin takes it back with William Longsword's men. Arnulf has William killed at Picquigny (17 December 942) and takes Montreuil again (948).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The mouth of the Canche, Quentovic's old water, is fought over for ten years. The crossing to Kent is safer from Flanders or from Rouen than from between them.

wars.who: King Louis IV and Hugh the Great for Normandy; then Otto I for Louis
wars.what: With the count of Rouen a child, heathen newcomers (Setric, Turmod) are put down by the king (943), who takes Rouen (944). A Dane, Harald of Bayeux, seizes the king at a parley on the Dives (13 July 945). Otto I and Louis besiege Rouen in 946 and fail.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Rouen shows it can stand a siege by two kings. Its Northmen are still half heathen and still have friends with fleets.

wars.who: Richard I of Normandy against Theobald of Blois and King Lothair
wars.what: Theobald takes Evreux and is beaten at the ford of Hermentruville by Rouen (962). Richard calls in Danes, who waste Theobald's land until peace is made; many then sail for Spain.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The Seine above Rouen is unsafe for some years. Captives and plunder from the Chartres country are sold at Rouen.

wars.who: King Lothair in Flanders
wars.what: On Arnulf I's death the king marches in and takes Arras, Douai and Saint-Amand, leaving the child Arnulf II the north.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Flanders shrinks back to the coast and the Lys for twenty years; Bruges and Ghent are its whole strength.

wars.who: King Lothair against the emperor Otto II
wars.what: Lothair rides on Aachen and nearly takes Otto at table (June 978). Otto marches to the walls of Paris with an army that sings Alleluia from Montmartre, cannot cross the Seine, and loses his baggage at the Aisne. Peace at Margut, 980.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: A season's fear on the Meuse and the Seine and no more. Lotharingia stays German.
wars.source: Richer III.68-81; Gesta episcoporum Cameracensium I.97-98

wars.who: Hugh Capet against Charles of Lorraine, the last Carolingian claimant
wars.what: Charles takes Laon (988) and Reims (989). Bishop Adalbero of Laon betrays him in his bed (March 991); he dies in prison at Orleans.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The new king holds little more than Paris, Orleans and Senlis. Everywhere else a merchant deals with a duke, a count or a bishop.

wars.who: the peasants of Normandy and their lords
wars.what: Early in Richard II's rule peasants across the duchy hold meetings to use woods and waters by their own rules. Count Rodulf seizes their spokesmen and has hands and feet cut off.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: No trade is stopped. It shows whose the rivers and woods are: fishing, timber and passage are the lord's to grant or sell.

wars.who: the counts of Rennes against the counts of Nantes and Anjou
wars.what: Two battles on the heath of Conquereuil (981, 27 June 992). In the second Fulk Nerra of Anjou kills Conan I.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Nantes leans on Anjou, Rennes on Normandy. The Loire trade and the Channel trade of Brittany have different masters.
wars.source: Richer IV.81-86; Glaber II.3; Chron. Nantes 42-45

wars.who: the emperor Henry II, with King Robert II and Duke Richard II, against Baldwin IV of Flanders
wars.what: Baldwin seizes Valenciennes on the imperial side of the Scheldt. The siege of 1006 fails; in 1007 Henry wastes the country to Ghent and Baldwin submits. He is later given Valenciennes and the Zeeland islands as the emperor's man.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The count of Flanders now holds both banks of the Scheldt mouths, under two lords. Whoever goes from the Rhine delta to Bruges passes his tolls.
wars.source: Thietmar VI.29; Gesta episcoporum Cameracensium I.114-115; Sigebert of Gembloux 1006, 1007 (?)

wars.who: Richard II of Normandy against Odo II of Blois
wars.what: A fight for the border fort of Tillieres. Richard hires two sea-kings, Olaf and Lacman; on the way they sack Dol in Brittany. King Robert makes peace; Olaf is baptised at Rouen.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The last time a duke at Rouen calls in a heathen fleet. The same years King Aethelred of the English sits in exile at Rouen.

wars.who: Baldwin (V) against his father Baldwin IV
wars.what: The son, newly married to the king's daughter, drives his father out; Duke Robert of Normandy brings the old count back. Father and son swear peace over relics at Oudenaarde (1030).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Two years in which the Flemish forts choose sides. The peace sworn at Oudenaarde is also the first peace of God in Flanders.
wars.source: WJ VI.6; Gesta episcoporum Cameracensium III.50 (?); Nicholas 1992

wars.who: Duke Robert of Normandy against Alan III of Brittany
wars.what: Robert builds a fort on the Couesnon and wastes the country round Dol. A fleet gathered at Fecamp for the exiled English princes is blown to Jersey and turned on Brittany instead. Alan does homage at Mont-Saint-Michel.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Brittany's north coast answers to Rouen. The Channel Islands are a Norman fleet's harbour.

wars.who: the Norman lords against each other, in the boy duke's name
wars.what: The duke's guardians are murdered one after another. With King Henry's help William beats the western lords at Val-es-Dunes by Caen (1047), and the Truce of God is sworn at Caen that October.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Twelve bad years on Norman roads; private forts take toll where they like. After 1047 the duke's peace and the bishops' truce stand together.

wars.who: Baldwin V of Flanders and Duke Godfrey of Lotharingia against the emperor Henry III
wars.what: The rebels burn the emperor's palace at Nijmegen (1047). In 1049 the emperor comes with the pope's curse, a Danish fleet and an English fleet lying at Sandwich to shut Baldwin in by sea; he submits at Aachen. War again 1050-1054 (the emperor before Lille). After Henry's death Baldwin keeps the lands east of the Scheldt and the islands.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: In 1049 the sea off Flanders is closed by two kings' ships. Nijmegen's palace lies burned. Bruges is the refuge of every English exile, and the place where their plunder is sold.
wars.source: ASC (C, D) 1049; Hermann of Reichenau 1047-1054; Lampert of Hersfeld 1047, 1056; Sigebert of Gembloux 1054

wars.who: King Henry I and Geoffrey of Anjou against William of Normandy
wars.what: Two invasions of Normandy: one French army is cut up at Mortemer (February 1054), the other caught half across the Dives at Varaville (August 1057).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The king is kept off the lower Seine for good. Rouen's river trade to Paris goes on under tolls at the border forts.

wars.who: William of Normandy against Maine (1063), Brittany (1064) and England (1066)
wars.what: Maine is taken; Conan II is chased from Dol to Dinan with Earl Harold in the duke's army. In 1066 the fleet gathers at the mouth of the Dives, moves on 12 September to Saint-Valery on the Somme, waits for the wind, and sails on the evening of 27 September.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Every hull on the Norman coast is built, bought or pressed for the crossing. Afterwards one lord holds both sides of the Channel. The men of Rouen already had their own wharf at Dowgate in London under King Edward (?).
wars.source: WP I.37-45, II.1-9; WJ VII.31-36; ASC (D, E) 1066; the Bayeux Tapestry

wars.who: Robert 'the Frisian' against his nephew Arnulf III and the countess Richilde
wars.what: Robert comes from Holland, wins at Cassel (22 February 1071); the boy count and William fitzOsbern, sent by King William, are killed.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Flanders and Holland are in one man's hands for a time; Flanders and Norman England are enemies.
wars.source: Lampert of Hersfeld 1071; Orderic Vitalis IV

raids.what: Ships fall on the islands off Aquitaine; about 105 raiders are killed on the shore. Which island is not said; Noirmoutier is the usual guess (?).

raids.who: a fleet of 200 ships sent by King Godfred of the Danes
raids.what: All the islands off Frisia are wasted, the Frisians beaten in three fights and made to pay 100 pounds of silver.

raids.where: Bouin, on the bay south of the Loire
raids.who: thirteen ships of pirates from the north
raids.what: Driven off in Flanders by the coast guard, they lose five men at the Seine mouth, then plunder Bouin and go home rich.
They waste part of Frisia, come by Utrecht to Dorestad, plunder everything, kill some, carry off others, burn part.
Dorestad wasted a second time. The emperor, angry, sets guards on the coast.
The island monastery of Saint Philibert attacked; Count Renaud of Herbauges fights them on the island in August. Next year the monks leave for good.
raids.source: AB 835; Ermentarius I, preface; Ademar III.16 (?)

raids.what: Antwerp burned.
The trading place at the mouth of the Meuse burned; tribute taken from the Frisians. Witla is not named again.
Dorestad and Frisia wasted a third time. King Horik sends word that it is not his doing, and complains that envoys of his were killed near Cologne; the emperor has the killers punished.
They fall on Walcheren without warning (17 June), kill Count Eggihard and the Dane Hemming, take many women captive and a great sum of money.
They go on to Dorestad and take tribute there. The emperor gives up his journey to Rome, comes to Nijmegen, holds an inquiry into his counts and orders ships built.

raids.who: Oscherus (Asgeir) with a fleet from the sea
raids.what: Rouen burned (14 May); Jumieges burned; Saint-Wandrille buys itself off for six pounds; monks from Saint-Denis ransom 68 captives for 26 pounds.
They come at first light, plunder, take captives, kill people of both sexes, and leave nothing standing but the houses that were bought off. The same fleet crosses to Hamwic.

raids.who: Northmen, called Westfaldingi in one annal
raids.what: On Saint John's day (24 June) they storm the town crowded for the feast and kill Bishop Gunhard in his church. They winter on an island, bringing houses from the mainland 'as if to stay for ever'.

raids.where: the Garonne, as far as Toulouse
raids.what: They row up the Garonne to Toulouse, plundering both banks unopposed, then go on to Galicia and Seville.

Up the Seine in March. They hang 111 captives in sight of the king's army, reach Paris on Easter eve (28 March), plunder the empty town and Saint-Germain on Easter day, and leave for 7,000 pounds of silver.
raids.source: AB 845; Translatio S. Germani (the hanging and the days) (?); AX 845

raids.what: Three battles in Frisia in one year: the Frisians win the first and lose the next two.
Seguin, count of Bordeaux and Saintes, is caught and killed; Saintes is burned.
raids.source: AB 845; Lupus of Ferrieres ep. 31; Ademar III.17

raids.what: They take what tribute they like from Frisia and burn Dorestad and two other villages in sight of Lothar at Nijmegen, who cannot punish them.
They seize and hold Dorestad and the island of the Betuwe. The same year other Danes beat Nominoe of the Bretons three times; he pays them to go.
Bordeaux falls after a long siege, by night, is wasted and burned; the Annals of Saint-Bertin blame treachery by Jews of the town. The same fleet burns Melle, the silver-mining town and mint.

raids.where: the coast of Flanders (the Mempisc and the country of Therouanne)
raids.who: Northmen, part of the fleet that came with Rorik
raids.what: While Rorik takes Dorestad, the rest plunder the sea coast of the Menapii and the men of Therouanne; others cross to England.
They waste Frisia and the Betuwe, come up the Scheldt and burn the abbey of Saint Bavo at Ghent.
The Seine fleet lies from October 851 to June 852: Saint-Wandrille burned (9 January), Beauvais burned, a band cut up on its way back at Vardes.
They come to Frisia, take as much money as they ask, and go elsewhere.

raids.who: Northmen from the Seine (Godfrid, Sidroc) and others
raids.what: After a winter at Jeufosse on the Seine they move to the Loire: Nantes, Saint-Florent, and on 8 November Tours, where Saint Martin's is burned. The saint's body had been moved in time.
Blois burned. Bishops Agius of Orleans and Burchard of Chartres man ships and soldiers and turn them back from Orleans.
Bordeaux attacked again; the Loire fleet marches on Poitiers on foot and is beaten.

raids.who: Danes, a new fleet on the Seine from mid-August
raids.what: Orleans is sacked on 18 April by the Loire men. The Seine fleet winters at Jeufosse and on 28 December enters Paris and burns it. Three churches buy themselves off 'for a great sum of solidi'.

raids.who: Danes other than Rorik's, while he is away at the Eider
raids.what: They storm Dorestad and waste the Betuwe and the country round.
Utrecht is wrecked; Bishop Hunger and his clergy flee, first to Sint Odilienberg (given them by Lothar II in 858), then to Deventer.
raids.source: Lothar II's charter of 2 January 858 (OSU) (?); AB 857

raids.what: Abbot Louis of Saint-Denis and his brother Gauzlin are taken; the ransom, 686 pounds of gold and 3,250 of silver, strips the church treasuries. The king besieges Oissel from July to September and gives up.

raids.who: Danes from the Seine and a new fleet on the Somme
raids.what: Noyon is taken by night and Bishop Immo killed on the road; Saint-Valery and Amiens burned. Between Seine and Loire the common people swear a band against the Danes and are cut down by their own lords.

In January Paris and Saint-Germain are burned again, and merchants fleeing up the Seine by ship are chased and caught. Weland's Somme fleet, hired by the king for 5,000 pounds, cattle and corn, then besieges the Seine men on Oissel; they pay him 6,000 pounds and all winter together along the river.
They row up the Marne and burn Meaux. The king rebuilds the bridge at Trilbardou behind them; trapped, they give back captives and promise to leave.

In January, in a winter of floods, they come up the Rhine, waste Dorestad and a large estate where the Frisians had fled, kill many Frisian merchants and take a great crowd captive; then go up to an island by Neuss. They leave on Rorik's advice.
Saint Victor's at Xanten is burned; the provost flees with the saint's body to Cologne.
raids.source: AX 864 (its years run one ahead here)

raids.what: They land in Flanders, are thrown back by the people of the country, and go up the Rhine instead. Lothar II raises four pence from every holding to pay the Northman Rodulf.
Fleury and Orleans burned; Poitiers burned; on 20 October the Seine men enter Saint-Denis and plunder it for some twenty days.
They row to Melun; the king's men run without a fight. Peace is bought for 4,000 pounds of silver and wine, raised by a levy on every holding and a tenth of what merchants own. They sail in July.

They had taken the empty town to live in with wives and children. King Charles and Salomon besiege it; they give hostages and ask leave to stay on an island in the Loire until February and hold a market there.
He demands tribute from Count Albdag's Frisians. They answer that they owe tribute to King Louis and his sons only, fight, and kill him and 500 or 800 of his men.

raids.who: Northmen with about a hundred large ships 'which our people call bargae'
raids.what: They enter the Seine on 16 September. Next year the king raises 5,000 pounds of silver by weight to pay them.
It crosses in mid-July, burns Therouanne, wastes Brabant, and in November makes its winter camp in the abbey at Ghent, where it stays a year.
They take the king's palace at Nijmegen and wall it. Louis the Younger cannot storm it; they leave in the spring and burn it behind them.
Winter camp at Courtrai. On 28 December they burn Saint-Vaast at Arras; in the new year Cambrai, the Somme abbeys, Amiens and Corbie.

raids.who: the great army from its camp at Elsloo on the Meuse
raids.what: After their defeat at Saucourt (3 August) they move to the Meuse. That winter Liege, Maastricht, Tongeren, Cologne, Bonn, Zuelpich, Juelich and Neuss burn; at Aachen they stable horses in the king's chapel.
The port 'called Taventeri in the Frisian tongue', where Saint Lebuin lies, is burned with many killed. Trier is taken on Maundy Thursday (5 April).

raids.who: Northmen come up the Rhine with Godfrid's leave
raids.what: They wall themselves in at Duisburg and winter there; Count Henry hems them in and they burn the camp and go in the spring of 884.

raids.where: Amiens, and all Francia to the Seine
raids.what: From Amiens they take 12,000 pounds of silver, paid in October, burn their camp and march to Boulogne; part cross to Kent, part go to Leuven.
The Frisians beat a landing at Norden with great slaughter.
They enter Rouen on 25 July, break the Franks at the bridge of Pont-de-l'Arche, and row on.

raids.who: the great army; Sigfrid speaks for it
raids.what: They ask only to pass the bridges; refused, they besiege the island from 24 November 885. Bishop Gozlin buys Sigfrid off with 60 pounds in spring 886; the rest stay until the emperor gives 700 pounds and leave to winter in Burgundy.
Meaux falls after a siege; the town is burned and its people led away. Paris pays again in 889 to be left alone.
Saint-Lo is taken and its people killed with the bishop of Coutances. Alan of Vannes beats them; of 15,000, Regino says, 400 got back to the ships.
After the defeat on the Dyle and a year of famine it takes ship at Boulogne, 250 ships, horses and all, for Kent.

raids.who: Hundeus with five large ships, soon many more
raids.what: They enter the Seine, winter at Choisy on the Oise, raid to the Meuse. The king has Hundeus baptised at Easter 897.
Saint Martin's and 28 other churches at Tours burned (30 June).
raids.source: a note in a Tours manuscript, printed with the Annales of Saint-Martin (?)

raids.what: He besieges Chartres and is beaten off on 20 July; the bishop carries the Virgin's shift on the wall. The king's grant of Rouen follows.
raids.source: Dudo II.22-25; Annales of Sainte-Colombe of Sens 911

raids.what: The abbey at the western end of Brittany is destroyed; its monks carry Saint Guenole's body to Montreuil on the Canche.
raids.source: a note in the abbey's calendar (Copenhagen, Thott 239) (?); Price 1989

raids.who: Ragenold and the Northmen of the Loire
raids.what: All Brittany is wasted and trodden down, the Bretons 'sold, led away or driven out'; counts and monks cross to England. Nantes is their seat until 937.
They break the peace, raid the Beauvais and Amiens country; Amiens and Arras burn. The Franks cross the Seine and burn their farms, and storm their fort at Eu.
The Bretons, quarrelling among themselves, are beaten; Dol is taken and its bishop crushed to death in the press of people fleeing into the church.

raids.who: an English fleet sent by King Aethelred (?)
raids.what: It lands to burn the country and is destroyed by the men of the Cotentin under Nigel. Only the Norman writer tells it.
A year after burning Tiel (1006) the fleet comes up the Lek to Utrecht; the townsmen burn their own harbour quarter before it can be used against them. The raiders spare the town.

raids.who: Olaf (the later saint) and Lacman, hired by Duke Richard II
raids.what: On their way to Rouen they storm and burn Dol. Olaf is then baptised at Rouen by Archbishop Robert.

A fleet lands in Poitou; Duke William's night attack fails in the pits they dug for his horses; captives are ransomed. Some years earlier the viscountess of Limoges was carried off from the same coast and held three years.

raids.where: Flanders (as the market, not the victim)
raids.what: They plunder Sandwich and Essex, taking men, gold and silver, then go 'to Baldwin's land' and sell what they have taken.

laws.what: Capitulary of Herstal: slaves are to be sold only before the bishop or count or good witnesses, never beyond the march; no mail coats to be sold outside the kingdom.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A sale of people without the count's witness is void and dangerous. Carrying mail abroad is forbidden long before the Northmen come.

laws.what: Charles frees the men of Saint-Germain-des-Pres from toll at Rouen, Quentovic, Amiens, Maastricht and Dorestad.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Abbey ships pass the king's tollmen free; yours do not. Carrying for an abbey is worth more than the freight.

laws.what: Admonitio generalis: equal measures and just, equal weights in towns and monasteries; no usury; no servile work, market or lawsuit on Sunday.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A lender may not take more than he gave. Sunday trade is a sin and can be fined.

laws.what: After the quarrel with King Offa over a marriage, Charles forbids anyone from Britain and the English to land on the coast of Gaul to trade; Abbot Gervold, the king's toll-collector at Quentovic, talks him round.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A king can close the Channel ports with a word. In 793 the peace is new and the tollmen remember.

laws.what: Synod of Frankfurt: the top price of a modius of oats is 1 penny, barley 2, rye 3, wheat 4; the king's own grain goes cheaper. The new pennies with the king's name must be taken everywhere; who refuses pays 15 solidi.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Grain may not be sold dearer in plenty or in dearth. A good new penny cannot be refused; the old light ones go to the mint.

laws.what: Charles's letter to Offa: merchants of each kingdom have the king's protection in the other 'by the old custom of trading' and may appeal to the king; true pilgrims go free, but traders dressed as pilgrims pay toll. He asks that English cloaks be the old length, and answers Offa about the black stones.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The Channel is open again and a wronged merchant has a court to go to. Do not hide goods in a pilgrim's pack.

laws.what: The law of the Frisians is written down at about the time of the Aachen assembly: blood-prices and fines by rank, different in the three parts of Frisia (Sincfal to Vlie, Vlie to Lauwers, Lauwers to Weser).
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A Frisian is judged by Frisian law wherever he trades in the realm, and his blood-price depends on which side of the Vlie he was born.
laws.source: Lex Frisionum (MGH Fontes iuris 12); Einhard VK 29; Ann. Lauresh. 802 (?)

laws.what: No arm-rings or mail coats are to be given or sold to merchants.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Lords may not pay you in war gear. The king wants mail on his own men's backs.

laws.what: Capitulary of Thionville: merchants going to the Slavs and Avars may go no further than Bardowick, Schezla, Magdeburg, Erfurt, Hallstadt, Forchheim, Pfreimd, Regensburg and Lorch, each under a named officer; no arms or mail to be carried for sale, on pain of losing the whole cargo. Only old and just tolls may be taken; none where no bridge, ferry or help is given.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The eastern frontier is nine gates. A new toll invented by a count is unlawful and can be refused before the king's missi.

laws.what: Capitulary of Nijmegen: usury is 'to ask back more than was given'; 'filthy gain' is to buy corn or wine at harvest only to sell it dear. In this famine year a modius of oats is at most 2 pennies, barley 3, rye 4, wheat 6.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Buying for your own need or to share is trade; buying up at harvest to hoard is a crime. In a famine the price is capped and food may not leave the realm.

laws.what: No one may sell the best double cloak above 20 solidi or a single one above 10; a coat lined with marten or otter above 30, with the lesser fur called sismusinum above 10. Fine: 60 solidi.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The king caps the price of the Frisian's best wares. Charles thought the new short cloaks a cheat at the old price.
laws.source: MGH Capit. I no. 52 c. 5; Notker I.34

laws.what: No Sunday market except where there was one of old. No toll to be taken on a road or water where the traveller gets no bridge, ferry or help for it.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A Sunday market is lawful only if it is old. Tolls are a payment for a service.

laws.what: Capitulary of Boulogne: lords are to go with the fleet themselves when ships are sent out; no bishop or abbot may give or sell a mail coat or sword to anyone but his own men.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Ships and shipmen on the coast can be called to the king's fleet.

laws.what: Louis confirms to Saint Martin's of Utrecht its tenth of the king's income at Dorestad and its river-bank plots there: its men on the banks owe no dues, no one may lodge in their houses by force or seize their goods at death.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A tenth of every toll you pay at Dorestad goes to the bishop. The church's bank tenants are the best protected men on the quay.

laws.what: Louis's rules on tolls: toll only at markets where common wares are bought and sold, and at old bridges; none in open country, none on a ship that only passes or ties up for a few nights, none from a man carrying his own goods between his houses, to the palace or to the host.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A ship that only passes under a bridge or lies a night at a bank owes nothing. The tollman may ask only where you sell.

laws.what: The new pennies (the temple type, one stamp for the whole empire) are to be the only coin from Martinmas; counts who let the old run lose their office (?).
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: After 11 November old pennies are bullion. The mint keeps its cut when you change them.
laws.source: MGH Capit. I no. 150 c. 20; MEC 1

laws.what: The emperor's letter for his merchants (praeceptum negotiatorum): they come to the palace in mid-May every year or second year and serve his chamber; they owe no toll anywhere, except the tenth at Quentovic, Dorestad and the Alpine gates; no one may seize their ships for the king's service, call them to the host, or judge them except before the emperor or the master of the merchants.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The best thing a merchant can own. It cannot free you of the tenth at Dorestad, but it keeps your ship from being pressed and your case out of the count's court.

laws.what: Louis frees the men of the church of Strasbourg from toll throughout the realm, except at Quentovic, Dorestad and the Alpine gates.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The same three exceptions as in 828: the king never gives away his tenth at the two sea gates.
laws.source: charter of 6 June 831 (Regesta Imperii I no. 890) (?)

laws.what: Lothar takes the Dane Rorik into his faith and grants him Dorestad and other counties, on terms: he is to handle the king's taxes and dues faithfully and hold off the Danish pirates.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The man who takes the king's tenth at Dorestad is now a baptised or half-baptised sea-king. His peace is real as long as he is at home.

laws.what: To pay the Northman Weland, Charles the Bald orders a levy on church treasures, on every holding, and on merchants, 'even the poorest': their houses and all their gear are valued and taxed.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: When the king buys peace, the merchant is assessed on everything he owns, not on what he sells.

laws.what: Edict of Pitres, the coin: new pennies with the king's name round his monogram, and the mint's name round a cross, struck only at the palace, Quentovic, Rouen, Reims, Sens, Paris, Orleans, Chalon, Melle and Narbonne. From 1 July (?) the new coin must be taken; after Martinmas only the new is lawful. Who refuses a good penny pays the king's ban of 60 solidi if free, and is flogged if not. Forgers lose a hand.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Change your silver before 11 November 864. Pennies found on you after that are cut up and you are fined.

laws.what: Edict of Pitres, markets and measures: each count is to list the markets in his county and say by whose leave each is held; markets set up without leave are closed; no market on Sunday. The measure is the one kept at the palace. A pound of refined gold may not be sold above 12 pounds of new pennies.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A market that is not on the count's list is no market: goods sold there can be seized.

laws.what: Edict of Pitres, the Northmen: whoever gives or sells a mail coat, any weapon or a horse to the Northmen, for ransom or any price, dies as a traitor to his country, with no buying off. Forts and hedged works raised without the king's leave are to be pulled down by 1 August. Fortified bridges are to close the rivers.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The one trade that costs your life. Even a horse given to ransom a kinsman counts.
laws.source: MGH Capit. II no. 273 c. 25 and the added chapter 1

laws.what: The tribute of 4,000 pounds: six pence from each free holding, three from each unfree, one from each cottar; a tenth of everything merchants are seen to own; from priests according to their means; the army fine from the free Franks.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A tenth of your whole stock, once, to buy the Seine men off. Free farmers pay pennies.

laws.what: The surrender at Angers: the Northmen may stay on an island in the Loire until February and hold a market there; then those baptised may stay, the rest must leave the kingdom.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: For one winter the king himself licenses a market with the Northmen. What they sell there was taken on the Loire.

laws.what: The tribute of 5,000 pounds, set at Compiegne (7 May): so many pence from each kind of holding; from merchants and those who live in towns, a levy according to what they have. At Quierzy (14 June) the king, leaving for Italy, promises that a dead count's son shall have his father's office.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Townsmen are taxed as a class for the first time. The count over you will be the old count's son: offices are becoming family land.
laws.source: MGH Capit. II no. 280, 281 c. 9; AB 877

laws.what: The peace of Asselt: Godfrid is baptised, marries Lothar II's daughter and receives the counties and benefices Rorik had held in Frisia; his fellow king Sigfrid takes more than 2,000 pounds of gold and silver, raised from church treasure.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Frisia has a Danish duke by the emperor's own gift. The Annals of Fulda tell that during the truce Franks went into the camp, some to trade and some to look; the Northmen shut the gates and killed them or held them for ransom.

laws.what: Carloman's capitulary of Ver against robbery: no one is to take by force on the road; priests are to give lodging to travellers; no one is to sell to a passer-by dearer than he sells in the market.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The last capitulary of a western king. Its market clause protects the traveller, on parchment.

laws.what: King Zwentibold gives the men of the church of Utrecht at Deventer and Tiel the same freedom from toll they used to have 'in Dorestad'.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Dorestad's rights have moved with its trade: to Deventer on the IJssel and Tiel on the Waal.

laws.what: King Charles grants Rollo Rouen and the land from the Epte to the sea 'for the defence of the kingdom'; Rollo is baptised. Dudo, a century later, adds Rollo's own law: a thief and whoever shelters him hang, so that a plough may be left in the field and a gold ring on a tree.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The Seine mouth has one lord who answers for theft. The plough and the ring are legend; the hard peace is not.
laws.source: charter of 14 March 918 (Recueil des actes de Charles III no. 92); Dudo II.28-32

laws.what: Kings give away their mints, markets and tolls: Odo grants a mint to the monks of Tournus (889), Charles the Simple a mint and market to Saint-Martin of Tours (919), and so on through the century.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: There is no longer one coin or one toll. Each abbot, bishop and count strikes and charges his own; the name on the penny is often a king long dead.
laws.source: MEC 1; Dumas 1973, 'Le debut de l'epoque feodale en France d'apres les monnaies' (?)

laws.what: Council of Charroux, the first Peace of God: cursed is whoever breaks into a church, robs a peasant or poor man of ox, cow, ass, sheep or pig, or strikes an unarmed cleric.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The bishops, not the king, now promise safety. In 989 the list does not yet name merchants.

laws.what: Treaty of Rouen (1 March), made by the pope's envoy Leo of Trier between King Aethelred and Richard I: neither is to receive the other's enemies or any of his men without his seal.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: It is aimed at Rouen's trade with the fleets raiding England. It does not hold: ten years later the Danes are selling there again.
laws.source: letter of Pope John XV in William of Malmesbury, Gesta regum II.166

laws.what: London's toll rules: the men of Rouen who come with wine or blubber-fish pay six shillings for a large ship and a twentieth of the fish; men of Flanders, Ponthieu, Normandy and Francia show their goods and pay toll.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: What a ship from Rouen or Bruges pays at Billingsgate. Wine is Rouen's cargo; the Flemings bring cloth.

laws.what: Richard II makes a lasting peace with King Sweyn of the Danes at Rouen: the Danes may bring their plunder to Normandy to sell, and their wounded are to be healed there. (The year is not given; it follows the English king's marriage to Emma in 1002.)
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Rouen is where English silver, church plate and captives come on the market. A poem of these years tells of an Irishman buying back his wife in the slave market of Rouen.
laws.source: WJ V.7 (?); Warner of Rouen, Moriuht (about 996-1026)

laws.what: The peace oath of Beauvais, drawn up by Bishop Warin for King Robert: 'I will not seize or rob merchants or pilgrims, nor take their goods, unless they do wrong.' The same clause is in the oath of Verdun-sur-le-Doubs (about 1020).
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: For the first time the armed men of a district swear by name not to rob merchants. An oath-breaker can be cursed and shut out of church.
laws.source: the oath text in Pfister, Etudes sur le regne de Robert le Pieux (1885), p. lx-lxi (?); Glaber IV.5

laws.what: Baldwin IV and the bishops have the peace sworn over the gathered relics of Flanders at Oudenaarde. In 1042-1043 the Truce of God is proclaimed for the diocese of Therouanne: no attack from Wednesday evening to Monday morning, and merchants and travellers are to have peace on all days (?).
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: In Flanders the count enforces the bishops' peace. Roads to his markets are under it.
laws.source: Gesta episcoporum Cameracensium III.50-54; the truce text of Therouanne (MGH Const. I no. 422) (?)

laws.what: The abbey of Saint-Vaast has its market toll at Arras written down: so much on each cartload, pack and ship's cargo, on wine, iron, cloth, wool and on a slave or slave woman (?).
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The first written tariff of a Flemish market. Tolls are now the abbot's or the count's, and listed item by item.
laws.source: Cartulaire de l'abbaye de Saint-Vaast (ed. Van Drival 1875), the toll list ascribed to Abbot Leduin (?)

laws.what: Council of Caen: the Truce of God for Normandy, sworn on relics brought from Rouen. No fighting from Wednesday evening to Monday morning, nor in Advent, Lent, or from Rogations to the week after Pentecost. The duke and the king are not bound.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Thursday to Sunday the roads are the safest they have been since Charles. The duke hangs those who break it.
laws.source: WJ VII.17 (?); Mansi XIX col. 597-600; Bates 1982

laws.what: Waiting a month at the Dives, Duke William feeds his army at his own cost and forbids all taking: 'the cattle and flocks of the country grazed safely', and the corn stood unharmed.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: An army that pays. Whoever has corn, wine or a hull to sell on the Norman coast in August 1066 is paid in the duke's silver.

coins.what: The light silver penny of Charles's early reign, about 1.3 g: CARO/LVS in two lines, the mint on the other side (Dorestad's with an axe). Twelve to the solidus, twenty solidi to the pound, both only counting words.
coins.mints: Dorestad, Quentovic, Melle, Mainz, Cologne, Paris, Rouen, Tours, Bordeaux and many more

coins.what: The heavy penny, about 1.7 g, 240 from a new pound of about 408 g: CARLVS REX FR round a cross, the KAROLVS monogram and the mint's name. Made lawful everywhere at Frankfurt in 794. There is a halfpenny (obol). The Frisian coast went on using the light weight for a time.
coins.mints: about forty: Dorestad, Quentovic, Rouen, Paris, Melle, Tours, Bordeaux, Mainz, Cologne
coins.source: MGH Capit. I no. 28 c. 5; MEC 1 p. 208-210; Coupland 2007

coins.what: The portrait penny: the emperor's head in a laurel wreath, KAROLVS IMP AVG. On the back a temple, or a mint's own sign: a ship for Dorestad and Quentovic, a town gate, the moneyer's tools for Melle. Rare; a coin for show after the Greeks recognised the title.
coins.mints: Aachen (?), Dorestad, Quentovic, Melle, Arles, Lyon, Rouen, Trier

coins.what: Louis the Pious, first and second issues: to 818 his portrait with the ship (Dorestad, Quentovic) or gate; 818 to 822/3 his name round a cross and the mint's name written across the field (DOR/ESTA/TVS).
coins.mints: about forty-five (?), Dorestad and Melle the busiest
coins.source: Coupland, 'Money and coinage under Louis the Pious', Francia 17 (1990); MEC 1

coins.what: The temple penny: HLVDOVVICVS IMP round a cross, XPISTIANA RELIGIO round a temple, and no mint name: one coin for the whole empire, about 1.7 g and good silver. Old pennies are out of law from Martinmas 825. It is copied for decades after his death, on the Frisian coast most of all.
coins.mints: all the mints, unnamed; Dorestad alone is known from some 450 dies
coins.source: MGH Capit. I no. 150 c. 20; Coupland 1990; dossiers/dorestad.md

coins.what: Gold: Louis has a few gold solidi struck, with his portrait and MVNVS DIVINVM ('God's gift'). They are copied in Frisia in gold, and the copies travel to England and the north. Gold is a gift and an ornament, not money for buying.
coins.mints: the palace (?); the copies in Frisia
coins.source: Grierson, 'The gold solidus of Louis the Pious and its imitations', Jaarboek voor Munt- en Penningkunde 38 (1951); MEC 1 p. 329

coins.what: Lothar I's pennies of Dorestad (DORESTATVS MON round a temple or cross): plentiful, and from about 850 light, base and badly cut, probably struck under Rorik. The mint stops with the town. The Frisians go on making blundered copies of Louis's temple penny.
coins.source: Coupland, 'Dorestad in the ninth century: the numismatic evidence', Jaarboek voor Munt- en Penningkunde 75 (1988); MEC 1

coins.what: Charles the Bald's first coinages, and Pippin II's in Aquitaine: each region keeps its own type (temple, mint name, monogram), weights slip and in places the silver falls to half. Melle, the mine and mint of Poitou, is burned by the Northmen in 848 and works again.
coins.mints: Paris, Orleans, Reims, Sens, Rouen, Quentovic, Melle, Bordeaux, Toulouse, Bourges and others
coins.source: Coupland, 'The early coinage of Charles the Bald', Numismatic Chronicle 151 (1991); AB 848

coins.what: The penny of the Edict of Pitres: +GRATIA D-I REX round the KAROLVS monogram, the mint's name round a cross; back to about 1.7 g of good silver. The edict names ten mints; in fact more than a hundred places strike it, most of them north of the Seine. Odo (ODO REX) and Charles the Simple keep the pattern.
coins.mints: named in 864: the palace, Quentovic, Rouen, Reims, Sens, Paris, Orleans, Chalon, Melle, Narbonne
coins.source: MGH Capit. II no. 273 c. 10-12; Grierson, 'The Gratia Dei Rex coinage of Charles the Bald' (1990); MEC 1 p. 232-235

coins.what: Silver that leaves: the tributes on record are 7,000 pounds (845), 5,000 (861), 4,000 (866), 5,000 (877), 12,000 (884), 700 (886), and sums not stated or paid by others in 853 (?), 862, 889, 897, 924 and 926; besides church ransoms such as Saint-Denis's 686 pounds of gold and 3,250 of silver (858). In 877 it is paid 'by weight'. Few of these pennies are found in the north: most were melted for rings and ingots.

Frozen types: the mints pass to counts, bishops and abbots, who go on striking a dead king's stamp, ever lighter and rougher. Melle's CARLVS REX FR and Le Mans's monogram run for two hundred years. A penny is now known by its town ('of Rouen', 'of Paris', 'of Le Mans'), and each has its own worth.
coins.mints: every county town and many abbeys

coins.what: Rouen: the first pennies in a Norman ruler's name are William Longsword's (VVILELMVS), then Richard I's (RICARDVS, with the mint ROTOMAGVS). The great hoard hidden at Fecamp about 980-985 holds some 8,500 pennies, most of them Rouen's. By the 1050s the Rouen penny is small and base, and English pennies are the good silver on the quay.
coins.source: Dumas, Le tresor de Fecamp et le monnayage en Francie occidentale (1971); Bates 1982 p. 96-97

coins.what: Flanders: small light pennies in the count's name, from Arnulf II (?) and surely from Baldwin IV, with the name of the town. They stay small while German and English pennies grow: a Flemish penny is under a gram.
coins.mints: Bruges, Ghent, Arras, Saint-Omer; later Lille (?)
coins.source: Nicholas 1992; Ghyssens, Les petits deniers de Flandre (1971) (?)

coins.what: The king's own penny, struck in his few towns, the forerunner of the 'penny of Paris'. Outside the Seine and Loire country nobody has to take it. A merchant crossing France changes money at every lordship.
coins.source: MEC 1; Lafaurie, Les monnaies des rois de France I (1951) (?)

coins.what: Brittany: Rennes and Nantes strike Charles the Bald's monogram penny after 864 and keep its stamp for generations; the Breton rulers put no name of their own on coin until the 11th century (?). Under the Northmen (919-937) Nantes strikes nothing.

church.what: Charles gives Saint Martin's of Utrecht the church called Upkirika above Dorestad, with land, the bank-due on the Lek and an island between Rhine and Lek.

Liudger is given the five Frisian districts east of the Lauwers to preach in; driven out by the rising of 784 and again troubled in 793, he ends as first bishop of Muenster (805) and dies in 809. The blind Frisian singer Bernlef is his convert.
Synod of Frankfurt: the Spanish teaching that Christ was God's adopted son is condemned, the Greeks' council on images rejected; the same assembly fixes prices and the new penny.
Pope Leo crowns Charles emperor in Saint Peter's on Christmas Day.
Five reform councils (Mainz, Reims, Tours, Chalon, Arles). Tours orders priests to preach in the people's own speech, 'the rustic Roman tongue or the German'.
Councils at Aachen (816-819) under Louis and Benedict of Aniane: one rule, Benedict's, for every monastery; a rule for canons.

The monks of Saint Philibert on Noirmoutier get leave to build a refuge on the mainland at Deas, because of 'the frequent and untimely coming of the barbarians'; from then they spend only the winters on the island.
church.source: charter of Louis the Pious, 16 March 819 (?); Ermentarius I, preface

church.what: Harald, exiled king of the Danes, is baptised at Saint Alban's by Mainz with his wife and some 400 followers; the emperor stands godfather. The monk Ansgar goes north with him, by ship down the Rhine past Dorestad.
church.source: ARF 826; Ermold IV; Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 7

church.what: Louis the Pious, deserted by his army, does public penance before the bishops at Saint-Medard of Soissons and lays his sword-belt on the altar. He takes it up again in 834.
The monks carry Saint Philibert's body off Noirmoutier (7 June) to Deas. They move again to Cunault (858), Messais (862) and at last Tournus in Burgundy (875).
Bishop Gunhard of Nantes is killed at the altar on Saint John's day with his clergy and people.
Hincmar becomes archbishop of Reims (to 882): the king's chief counsellor, and from 861 the writer of the Annals of Saint-Bertin.
Nominoe puts out the Frankish bishops of Brittany at Coitlouh and sets up Dol as the Bretons' own archbishop's see, free of Tours. Rome never agrees; the quarrel runs past 1066.
church.source: Chron. Nantes 11; letters of Popes Leo IV and Nicholas I (?)

church.what: Saint Martin's body is carried out of Tours before the Northmen burn his church (8 November); it comes home, leaves again, and is not settled until the 880s.
church.source: AB 853; Odo of Cluny (?), De reversione beati Martini (legendary in detail)

church.what: Bishop Hunger and the clergy of Utrecht flee the Northmen. The see sits at Deventer for some sixty years, until Bishop Balderic brings it back about 920.

Pope Nicholas I pleads for Baldwin and Judith, the king's runaway daughter, 'lest he join the Northmen'; they are married at Auxerre. In the same years he forbids King Lothar II to put away his wife Theutberga for Waldrada; Lothar dies without a lawful heir and his kingdom is carved up.
church.source: AB 862, 863, 865, 869; Nicholas I, letters (MGH Epp. VI)

church.what: The monks of Saint Philibert, forty years on the road from Noirmoutier, are given Tournus on the Saone. On Christmas Day Charles the Bald is crowned emperor at Rome.
church.source: charter of Charles the Bald, 19 March 875 (?); AB 875, 876

church.what: Hincmar, old and sick, flees Reims by night in a litter with Saint Remigius's body as the Northmen come near, and dies at Epernay (21 December).
church.source: AB 882 (his last entry); Flodoard HRE III.30

church.what: In the siege of Paris the bodies of Saint Germain and Saint Genevieve are carried along the walls; Bishop Gozlin dies in the plague (16 April).
Archbishop Fulk of Reims is killed on the road by Winemar, a man of Count Baldwin II (17 June). The bishops curse the killers; the count is not touched.
Duke William of Aquitaine founds the abbey of Cluny (11 September) and puts it under no lord but Saint Peter. Its customs spread through the next century.
church.source: Cluny's foundation charter (Recueil des chartes de Cluny I no. 112)

church.what: Rollo is baptised at Rouen by Archbishop Franco, taking the name Robert, and gives land to the churches of Rouen, Bayeux, Evreux, Jumieges, Mont-Saint-Michel and Saint-Denis, one a day for a week. The year and the gifts are Dudo's telling.

Breton monks leave with their saints before the Northmen: Saint Guenole's body goes from Landevennec to Montreuil, those of Samson, Malo and Magloire to Paris and Orleans, others over the sea to King Aethelstan.
Charles the Simple gives Count Dirk the church of Egmond and its land: the beginning of the abbey of Egmond, the house of the later counts of Holland.

Count Arnulf I brings in Gerard of Brogne to restore the monks' life at Saint Peter's in Ghent (941), then Saint-Bertin (944) and Saint Bavo. In 944 the bodies of Saints Wandrille, Ansbert and Wulfram, carried from the Seine in the raids, are brought into Saint Peter's.
church.source: Folcwin, Gesta abbatum S. Bertini 107; Annales Blandinienses 941, 944 (?)

church.what: William Longsword calls monks from Poitiers to rebuild Jumieges, burned in 841; he had wished to become a monk there himself.
Richard I puts Benedictine monks on Mont-Saint-Michel in place of the canons.
church.source: charter of King Lothair, 966 (?); the Introductio monachorum

church.what: The bishops of Aquitaine at Charroux proclaim the first Peace of God.
The council of Saint-Basle at Verzy deposes Archbishop Arnulf of Reims for treason to Hugh Capet; Gerbert of Aurillac is put in his place, loses it, and in 999 becomes pope as Sylvester II.
church.source: Gerbert, Acta concilii Remensis; Richer IV.51-73

church.what: Richard II brings William of Volpiano from Dijon to rule Fecamp, beside the duke's hall; from it Norman monasteries are reformed. Pilgrims come for the relic of Christ's blood.
At Orleans, before King Robert, a group of canons is condemned for heresy and burned: the first such burning in the West.
A thousand years from the Passion: after three years of famine a good harvest, peace councils everywhere, and 'a countless multitude' sets out for Jerusalem.
The knight Herluin founds the abbey of Bec; Lanfranc of Pavia comes to teach there about 1042.

Pope Leo IX holds a council at Reims against the king's wishes, deposes bishops who bought their office, and forbids Count Baldwin to give his daughter to William of Normandy. They marry all the same about 1051, and found the two abbeys at Caen as penance.
church.source: Anselm of Saint-Remi, Historia dedicationis; WJ VII.21, 26 (?)

church.what: Duke William sails under a banner sent by Pope Alexander II. While the fleet waits at Saint-Valery the saint's body is carried out of the church to pray for a south wind.
The new abbey church of Jumieges is dedicated on 1 July in the presence of King William, back from England.
